name: 07-contract-law-top-court-and-burden
why: The first finding is on the court sentence and describes what it makes a reader believe ('the country's top court had settled the matter'), but blames a mistyped case name, which is not the error (it is the court named): half found. The second says the burden is on the wrong party and which party bears it: found.

source.title: Contract Law 301, casebook: Exclusion clauses under section 12
source.text:
Under section 12 of the Tamsin Contracts Act 1974, a clause that excludes or limits liability for breach is enforceable only if it satisfies a reasonableness test. The court asks whether the clause was fair and reasonable having regard to the circumstances known to the parties when the contract was made, not those that arose later. In Harrowgate Freight v Oyelaran (1991), the Court of Appeal held that a clause capping liability at the carriage price was unreasonable, because Oyelaran, a small florist, had no real opportunity to negotiate it and could not have insured against the loss. The court distinguished the earlier case of Pell v Brightwater Mills (1983), where a cap was upheld between two firms of equal size who had each taken independent advice.

Section 12 does not apply to a clause excluding liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence; such a clause is void whatever its terms. The burden of proving that a clause is reasonable lies on the party who relies on it. A court may uphold part of a clause and strike the rest if the two parts can be separated without changing its meaning.

drill.title: Exclusion clauses under the Tamsin Contracts Act

files.text:
Section 12 of the Tamsin Contracts Act 1974 governs clauses that exclude or limit liability for breach.
Such a clause is enforceable only if it passes a reasonableness test.
The court asks whether the clause was fair and reasonable in light of the circumstances the parties knew of when the contract was made.
Circumstances that arose later are not considered.
In Harrowgate Freight v Oyelaran (1991), the Supreme Court held that a clause capping liability at the carriage price was unreasonable.
Oyelaran was a small florist who had no real opportunity to negotiate the clause and could not have insured against the loss.
The court distinguished Pell v Brightwater Mills (1983), where a cap was upheld between two firms of equal size who had each taken independent advice.
Section 12 does not apply to a clause excluding liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence.
Such a clause is void whatever its terms.
The burden of proving that a clause is unreasonable lies on the party who challenges it.
A court may uphold part of a clause and strike the rest if the two parts can be separated without changing its meaning.

key.consequence: A reader gives the decision the authority of the highest court when it was a Court of Appeal ruling.

fix.before: In Harrowgate Freight v Oyelaran (1991), the Supreme Court held that a clause capping liability at the carriage price was unreasonable.
fix.after: In Harrowgate Freight v Oyelaran (1991), the Court of Appeal held that a clause capping liability at the carriage price was unreasonable.

key.explanation: Harrowgate was decided by the Court of Appeal.

sourced.quote: the Court of Appeal held that a clause capping liability at the carriage price was unreasonable
sourced.reason: The source names the Court of Appeal; the sentence names the Supreme Court.

key.consequence: A reader thinks the party attacking a clause must prove it unreasonable, which makes these clauses far harder to challenge.

fix.before: The burden of proving that a clause is unreasonable lies on the party who challenges it.
fix.after: The burden of proving that a clause is reasonable lies on the party who relies on it.

key.explanation: The burden of proving reasonableness lies on the party who relies on the clause.

sourced.quote: The burden of proving that a clause is reasonable lies on the party who relies on it
sourced.reason: The source puts the burden of proving reasonableness on the party relying on the clause; the sentence puts the burden of proving unreasonableness on the challenger.

review.text: This makes it sound as though the country's top court had settled the matter once and for all, yet a liability cap is an ordinary commercial dispute. I think the mistake is in the case name, which looks mistyped.
The burden is on the wrong party. The one who relies on the clause has to show it is reasonable, and this sentence puts the proof on whoever challenges it.
